passage:
"Why are you crying, Sumit?" Urmila didi asked, putting down her books.
"Bunty won my blue marble! My best one!"
"But you won two of his this morning. You showed me."
"That was different." He sniffed hard. "Those were just marbles."
"And the blue one?"
"It was MINE."
"This morning you jumped once and ran off to play again."
"Because winning is okay. Losing is horrible."
Urmila didi smiled a little. "So today you're one marble up, and you feel like you lost everything."
Sumit thought about it, wiping his nose on his sleeve. "It still feels like I lost more," he said, and cried a bit more quietly.

qa.q: How many of Bunty's marbles had Sumit won that morning?
qa.a: Sumit had won two of his marbles that morning.

qa.q: Why does losing the blue marble feel worse to Sumit than winning two felt good?
qa.a: The blue marble was his own, so losing it feels like part of him is gone, while winning felt pleasant but small.

qa.q: How could Urmila didi help Sumit next time?
qa.a: She could comfort him first, then count the marbles with him so he sees he is still ahead, without telling him his feelings are wrong.

qa.q: How might Bunty feel about winning the blue marble?
qa.a: Bunty probably feels pleased and may not know the marble meant so much, since for Sumit the morning's wins barely counted.

grounding: Shows a boy crying harder over losing one marble than he celebrated winning two.

passage: Last summer I learned something about myself. I'm Mohit, and I love collecting cricket cards. One day at the park I won three cards from Sudha in a game. I said "yay" and put them in my box. That was it. The next day I lost one card to her, my old spinner card, the bent one. I cried all the way home. Mummy asked why. I said, "She took my card!" Mummy said, "But you still have two extra." I knew that, but it didn't feel like it. The lost card felt huge and the three new ones felt tiny. Now when I lose one, I try to remember the ones I won.

qa.q: How many cards did Mohit win from Sudha?
qa.a: Mohit won three cards from Sudha.

qa.q: Why did the bent spinner card feel so huge to Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit felt upset because it was his own card, so losing it hurt much more than winning three new ones felt good.

qa.q: What does Mohit try now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Mohit tries to remember the cards won whenever one is lost, which balances the painful feeling with the real count.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt seeing Mohit cry all the way home?
qa.a: Sudha might have felt confused or guilty, since Mohit had won three cards from her just the day before.

grounding: Shows a child for whom losing one owned card hurt far more than winning three new cards felt good.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3B. Shankar sir, Friday.
Observation: In today's maths game, each child started with five tokens and could win or lose one per round. When Lokesh won a token, he smiled briefly and moved on. When he lost one, he put his head on the desk and cried for several minutes, even though he finished with seven, more than he began with. He told me, "I lost my green one. It was mine from the start." Three other children reacted the same way.
What I did next: At the end, I asked the class to count their tokens aloud, and we talked about how losing can feel bigger than winning even when you're ahead. Lokesh counted twice and smiled a little.

qa.q: How many tokens did Lokesh finish with?
qa.a: Lokesh finished with seven tokens.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh cry for several minutes over one token?
qa.a: Lokesh felt sad and hurt because the green token was his from the start, so losing it felt like losing something of his own. That pain outweighed the tokens he had gained.

qa.q: Why was counting aloud a helpful step?
qa.a: It let the children see the real totals, so the loud feeling of loss could be checked against the fact that many were ahead.

qa.q: How might the other children who reacted the same way feel after the talk?
qa.a: They might feel relieved to learn that losing often feels bigger, and less embarrassed about crying. 🙂

grounding: Shows a boy crying hard over one lost token while barely noticing the ones he won, and a teacher helping the class see it.

passage:
Friday
Dear Diary,
At recess I played marbles with Shankar. I won his green cat's-eye marble! I said "yes!" and put it in my pocket. Then I kept playing. Then I lost my red one. My red one! The one Nana gave me. I cried so hard that Miss asked if I was hurt. I wasn't. I just felt terrible. Shankar said, "But you won the green one, so it's the same." It's NOT the same. The green one felt nice for a minute. Losing the red one felt bad for the whole day. I don't even know why. Mummy hugged me. "My poor boy. Losing feels bigger than winning, na?" Tomorrow I will ask Shankar if we can swap back. I'll give him his green one.
Madhav

qa.q: Who gave Madhav the red marble?
qa.a: Nana gave it to him.

qa.q: Why did losing the red marble feel worse to Madhav than winning the green one felt good?
qa.a: The red marble was his, and giving up something he owned felt much heavier than getting a new one, even though it was a fair swap. It also came from Nana.

qa.q: What does Madhav plan to do tomorrow, and why might it help?
qa.a: He plans to ask Shankar to swap back. Getting the red marble back would ease the loss, and it shows he can find a fair fix instead of staying upset.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about Madhav crying so much after the game?
qa.a: Shankar may feel confused, since to Shankar one marble for one marble is fair, and maybe a bit worried he did something wrong.

grounding: A boy writes in his diary that losing his marble made him cry harder than winning a marble made him happy.

passage: On Uttarayan morning in their village near Anand, Tushar, eight, stood on the roof with his sister Ganga and a stack of kites. By noon he had cut two kites from the neighbour's roof. Each time he shouted "Kaypo che!", danced a moment, and flew on. At two, a purple kite crossed his string, and snap, his favourite yellow kite drifted away over the fields. Tushar burst out crying. He sat by the water tank and wouldn't get up. "You cut two of theirs!" Ganga said. "That's two to one!" "That was mine," he sobbed. "The yellow one." Ganga sat beside him and gave him a sesame laddoo. "Losing yours feels bigger, na?" He nodded. After a while he picked up a red kite. "Tie it for me, didi?"

qa.q: How many kites had Tushar cut by noon?
qa.a: He had cut two kites from the neighbour's roof.

qa.q: Why did Tushar cry so much about his yellow kite when he had just won two?
qa.a: Tushar felt heartbroken because his own favourite kite was gone, and that loss felt heavier than the joy of cutting two of theirs.

qa.q: What helped Tushar get back to flying?
qa.a: Ganga sat with him, gave him a laddoo and named how losing feels bigger, instead of arguing that two beats one. Feeling understood let him pick up a new kite.

qa.q: If you were Ganga, why might Tushar's tears surprise you?
qa.a: You'd see that he was winning, two to one, so the tears seem out of proportion, until you notice how much the lost kite belonged to him.

grounding: On a kite-flying festival, a boy cries far harder over losing his kite than he celebrated cutting two others.

passage: Yesterday I won a blue cat's-eye marble from Tipu in the courtyard. I said "yes!", put it in my tin and went back to playing. That was it. Then, ten minutes later, I lost my red one to Chotu, the red one I've had since Diwali. I cried so much that Vinita didi came down from the terrace. She said, "Naveen, you won one and you lost one. You have the same number of marbles." I know. I counted. But the blue one felt like just a marble, and the red one felt like MINE. Losing it hurt way more than winning felt good. Didi said that's normal and gave me a hug. Today I still looked for the red one in Chotu's pocket.

qa.q: Since when had Naveen had the red marble?
qa.a: Since Diwali.

qa.q: Why did losing the red marble hurt more than winning the blue one felt good?
qa.a: The red one felt like Naveen's own, so losing it brought real hurt and tears, while the new blue one felt like just a marble.

qa.q: How does Vinita didi help, and what else could help Naveen?
qa.a: She points out the count is the same and gives a hug; Naveen could also give the blue marble time to feel special too.

qa.q: How might Chotu feel when Naveen checks his pocket?
qa.a: Chotu may feel a bit uncomfortable or annoyed, since he won the red marble fairly.

grounding: A child recalls crying hard over losing a marble after barely noticing winning an equal one.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3B, Friday
Something from our reward stars this week is worth recording about Darshan. On Monday he earned a gold star for his reading; he smiled, said "thank you, Miss," and went back to his seat. On Thursday, after talking during the test, he lost one star from his chart. He cried for almost twenty minutes and would not come out at break. Preeti, who sits next to him, told me, "He says it was his best star." It was the same star he had earned on Monday. I sat with him at lunch, told him that feeling upset about losing something is normal, and showed him how he could earn it back by Friday. He did. From now on I will be gentler about taking stars away.

qa.q: What did Darshan earn the gold star for on Monday?
qa.a: For his reading.

qa.q: Why did Darshan cry so much over one lost star?
qa.a: He felt hurt and upset because the star had become his own, so losing it felt far heavier than earning it had felt good.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Darshan?
qa.a: Sat with him at lunch, said feeling upset about losing is normal, and showed him a way to earn the star back by Friday.

qa.q: How does Preeti seem to see Darshan's upset?
qa.a: Preeti seems concerned for him, explaining to the teacher that he calls it his best star.

grounding: A teacher records a boy who barely reacts to earning a star but cries hard when he loses the same star.

passage:
Tuesday
Today I found a ten-rupee coin under the bench in the park. I was happy for about one minute and then I forgot about it.
In the evening Pradeep and I went to buy samosas, and I found out I had lost my own ten-rupee note, the one Nani gave me on Sunday. I was SO upset. I looked everywhere, even inside my socks. I didn't want my samosa. Pradeep said, "But you found ten rupees this morning, so it's the same." I know it's the same. Maths says it's the same. But the coin was just lucky, and the note was mine, from Nani. Losing it felt like losing something from my pocket and my heart.
Tomorrow I'll check under the bench again, just in case.
Deepak

qa.q: Who gave Deepak the ten-rupee note?
qa.a: Nani, on Sunday.

qa.q: Why was Deepak so upset about the note when a coin had been found the same day?
qa.a: The note felt like Deepak's own, from Nani, so losing it hurt far more than finding the lucky coin felt good.

qa.q: What could help Deepak feel better about the lost note?
qa.a: Telling Nani how much the note meant, and letting the coin found that morning feel like a small gift too.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the loss?
qa.a: Pradeep sees it as even, since ten rupees were found and ten were lost, and is puzzled that Deepak is so upset.

grounding: A child's diary shows losing a ten-rupee note hurting far more than finding an equal coin felt good.

passage: In their village near Palakkad, Darshan, eight, played marbles with his friend Jomon every evening under the tamarind tree. On Monday, Darshan won Jomon's blue marble. He smiled, put it in his pocket, and forgot about it by dinner. On Tuesday, he lost his own green marble, the one with the gold swirl, to Jomon. He burst into tears. He cried all the way home and wouldn't eat. His mother asked what happened. "Jomon took my green one!" "But you won his blue one yesterday." "That's different!" He hugged his knees on the verandah, sobbing. The blue marble sat forgotten in his pocket. The green one felt like it had been torn from him.

qa.q: What colour was the marble Darshan won on Monday?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: Why did losing the green marble hurt Darshan so much more than winning the blue one pleased him?
qa.a: Losing something he owned felt like it was torn away, so the hurt was much heavier than the small happiness of winning an equal marble.

qa.q: How could Darshan's mother help him feel better?
qa.a: She could let him cry, then gently remind him of the blue marble and suggest he can win the green one back another day.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel about winning the green marble?
qa.a: Jomon might feel pleased at first, then awkward seeing his friend so upset.

grounding: It shows a boy who cries harder over losing a marble than he celebrates winning one, as losing something owned feels heavier.

passage: In Seville, Pablo and his friend Siddiq traded football cards at the school gate every morning. On Monday, Pablo got a card he'd wanted from Siddiq in a trade. He said "cool" and put it in his album. On Wednesday, Siddiq asked for Pablo's goalkeeper card in exchange for an equally good striker. Pablo held the goalkeeper tight. "No way." "But the striker's just as good!" "It's mine." Siddiq finally talked him into it. Pablo handed it over and immediately felt awful. He sulked all day. He didn't even look at the new striker card. That night he asked his mother if he could trade it back. "Why? You got a good card." "But I lost my goalkeeper," he said, near tears.

qa.q: What card did Pablo give up on Wednesday?
qa.a: His goalkeeper card.

qa.q: Why did Pablo feel so bad after an equal trade?
qa.a: Giving up a card he owned felt like a painful loss, heavier than the pleasure of getting an equally good one, so he felt hurt and near tears.

qa.q: What could Pablo think about before trading next time?
qa.a: He could remind himself that losing a card usually feels worse than it is, and decide if the new card is really worth the same.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see Pablo's reaction?
qa.a: Siddiq may feel confused, since he offered an equally good card, and a bit annoyed if Pablo wants to trade back.

grounding: It shows a boy who feels much worse about giving up a card than he feels good about getting an equal one.

passage: In the Class 3 classroom, Francis had a collection of scented erasers. On Thursday, the class played a quiz game where the winner took an eraser from the loser. Francis won a strawberry eraser from Swati. He smiled, said "yes!" and forgot it. Then he lost his mango eraser to another boy. His face crumpled. He cried so hard the teacher came over. "But you won one too," she said kindly. "I don't care about that one! I want my mango!" Swati, whose eraser he had won, leaned over. "Now you know how I felt." Francis wiped his nose, still sniffling. The strawberry eraser lay on his desk, untouched. His mind was only on the one he had lost.

qa.q: What scent was the eraser Francis won from Swati?
qa.a: Strawberry.

qa.q: Why did Francis cry so hard over losing the mango eraser?
qa.a: Losing something he owned felt much heavier than winning an equal one, so he felt deeply hurt while the win barely registered.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Francis with this feeling?
qa.a: She could let him be sad, then talk about how losing often feels bigger than winning, and maybe suggest games without taking things.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Francis cries?
qa.a: Swati may feel a mix of sympathy and understanding, since she just lost her own eraser.

grounding: It shows a boy who cries harder over losing an eraser than he celebrates winning one, as losing something owned feels heavier.

passage:
Monday, summer holidays. Akash won a shiny blue marble from Zubin. He smiled, put it in his tin, and went back to playing.

Wednesday. Akash lost that same blue marble back to Zubin. He cried so hard his mother came running out. He sulked for the rest of the afternoon and wouldn't eat his mango.

Friday. Zubin sat next to him on the steps. "On Monday you won it, you didn't even jump. On Wednesday you lost it, you cried for an hour. It's the same marble."

Akash sniffed. "Losing it felt way worse."

"Why?"

"Because it was mine."

Zubin held out the blue marble. "Want to play again? Maybe you'll win."

Akash looked at it for a long time. "What if I lose again?"

qa.q: What colour was the marble?
qa.a: A shiny blue marble.

qa.q: Why did Akash cry so much when he lost the marble?
qa.a: Akash felt hurt and upset because the marble had become his, so losing it felt much heavier than winning it had felt good.

qa.q: What could Akash try if he plays again?
qa.a: Akash could remind himself that losing a marble is only the same as not having won it, so he can play and enjoy the game.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Akash's reaction?
qa.a: Zubin seems puzzled but kind, noticing the difference and offering to play again.

grounding: Over a few holiday days, a child barely celebrates winning a marble but cries hard when he loses it back.

passage:
Vikas, you're crying over losing one card, but you didn't smile when you won three? Let your Baljeet nanaji tell you about Lohri when I was eight.

That year I had a new red kite. I flew it once, for maybe ten minutes, and I thought, nice.

Then, the next day, it got stuck in the neighbour's tree and tore. I cried for the whole evening. I missed the bonfire.

My mother said something I didn't understand then. "When you got it, you were a little happy. When you lost it, you were very sad. Same kite."

Losing what's ours feels much heavier than getting something new.

So, Vikas, go back to your game. Maybe you'll win the card back. And if you don't, you still have three.

qa.q: What colour was young Baljeet's new kite?
qa.a: A new red kite.

qa.q: How did young Baljeet feel when the kite tore?
qa.a: Young Baljeet felt very sad and upset, crying all evening and missing the bonfire.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Baljeet's story?
qa.a: His mother's words about the same kite bringing little happiness but great sadness later helped him understand losses feel heavier.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's mother have felt watching him miss the bonfire?
qa.a: His mother probably felt sorry for him and wanted him to see the loss more clearly.

grounding: An elder recalls crying hard as a boy over a lost kite that had barely pleased him.

passage:
It was the Friday before Christmas holidays, and rain was hammering the school roof. The bus was leaving in five minutes. Chaitanya and Siddharth were trading football cards in the corridor.

Chaitanya won Siddharth's rare goalkeeper card. He shrugged. "Cool," and put it in his pocket.

Then he traded his own striker card for a defender. As soon as it was gone, his face crumpled. "I want it back."

"But it was mine!" Chaitanya's eyes filled with tears.

"You didn't even smile when you won my goalkeeper."

The bus honked. Chaitanya looked at the defender in his hand. It was just as good as the striker. But the striker had been his.

"Keep the striker," he muttered, wiping his eyes. "I'll trade for it after the holidays."

qa.q: Which card did Chaitanya win from Siddharth?
qa.a: Siddharth's rare goalkeeper card.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya feel so upset after trading the striker card?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt upset and sad because the striker had been his, so losing it felt much worse than winning the goalkeeper felt good.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try next time before trading?
qa.a: Chaitanya could pause and think whether the new card is just as good, and remember that it will feel like a loss for a moment.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel about Chaitanya's tears?
qa.a: Siddharth might feel confused and a bit annoyed, since Chaitanya didn't react when winning the goalkeeper.

grounding: Before a school holiday, a child barely reacts to winning a card but cries over trading away his own.

passage: Fog hung over the colony park in Ludhiana so thickly that the swings looked grey. Hemant and Gurpreet crouched beside a circle scratched in the cold dirt, fingers stiff inside their woollen gloves. Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring. He pocketed it with a small "yes" and moved on. Two turns later Gurpreet hit Hemant's blue-swirl marble clean out of the circle. Hemant's face crumpled. He sat back on his heels and wailed, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned around. "It's just one," said Gurpreet. "You won one of mine." "It's not the same!" Hemant sobbed, staring at his empty palm while the fog swallowed the far end of the park.

qa.q: What happened on Hemant's first shot?
qa.a: Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring.

qa.q: Why does losing the blue-swirl marble upset Hemant so much more than winning one pleased him?
qa.a: The blue-swirl marble was already his, so losing it feels like something taken away; he feels hurt and cheated, while the won marble only felt like a small extra.

qa.q: How could an adult help Hemant calm down?
qa.a: They could let him be sad for a moment, then point out that he won one and lost one, so he has the same number of marbles as when he started.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Hemant's crying?
qa.a: Gurpreet is puzzled, because to Gurpreet the game is even: Hemant won one marble and lost one.

grounding: Shows a child crying harder over losing a marble than he celebrated winning an equal one.
